Ultimatum game and trial-level signals

The ultimatum game is a classical social decision-making task, in which two players interact to divide a sum of money (Güth et al., 1982; Güth & Kocher, 2014). Participants played as the responder. On each trial, they decided whether to accept or reject a monetary offer from a proposer. Before receiving the offer, participants predicted the amount they expected to receive and rated their predicted feelings about the exchange; after receiving the offer, they rated their experienced feelings. The task yields two trial-level prediction-error signals per offer. The reward prediction error is the received minus the predicted monetary amount, whereas the emotion prediction error is the experienced minus the predicted valence rating. We used the valence prediction error only and did not enter the arousal prediction error in any model. Valence prediction errors predicted social choices across task contexts, whereas the effect of arousal prediction errors depended on the context (Heffner et al., 2021). Supplement S1 maps both signals to the variables in the released dataset. We used the reward and valence prediction errors as scaled in the released data (Heffner et al., 2021). Each was divided by a single standard deviation computed over all trials pooled across the participants, without mean-centering.

Mean-contrast decomposition

We split each trial's two prediction errors into the part they share and the part on which they diverge, their mean and their contrast. Across trials the two standardized signals are strongly correlated (r = .757), so their separate drift weights compete for the same variance.

Because each prediction error is standardized to unit variance over the pooled data, the mean and the contrast are uncorrelated across that pooled sample, however strongly RPE and EPE are correlated. Positive contrast marks a monetary outcome above the emotional one.Within participants the two signals span a wider range. Supplement S1 reports the within-participant correlation and the variance inflation factor,

Standard drift-diffusion model

We modeled choice and response time jointly with a drift-diffusion process, in which noisy evidence accumulates until it reaches one of two boundaries (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008).

Evidence starts between the boundaries, accumulates at a mean rate (i.e., the drift rate), and the first boundary reached determines both the choice and its latency. We assigned acceptance to the upper boundary and rejection to the lower, so that a positive drift indexes a propensity to accept.

The primary parameters compared between groups are drift rate,which indexes the rate and direction of evidence accumulation, and decision threshold, which indexes the evidence required before committing to a choice. The model also estimates non-decision time, which is defined as the response time spent on stimulus encoding and motor execution outside the decision process.

We fitted the model by evaluating the joint likelihood of choice and response time deterministically using the Navarro-Fuss series for the Wiener first-passage-time density (Navarro & Fuss, 2009), rather than by simulating the diffusion process. A deterministic likelihood avoids the Monte-Carlo noise in the likelihood surface, which is especially important when each participant contributes relatively few trials.

To keep the remaining parameters identifiable, we fixed several quantities. The starting point was fixed at the unbiased midpoint (Voss et al., 2015), the diffusion coefficient σ was fixed at 1.4 as a scaling convention, and across-trial variability in drift rate, starting point, and nondecision time was fixed to zero. The implementation details and all fixed and bounded parameter values are shown in Supplement S1.

Time-varying drift-diffusion model

Asking when an attribute begins to influence a decision requires a time-varying DDM (Maier et al., 2020), in which the drift switches at τ. Before τ the mean signal alone drives accumulation, and at τ the contrast signal is added (Figure 1c).

Because the drift changes at τ, the likelihood of a response made after τ depends on the evidence level at τ. We therefore computed the distribution of evidence levels at τ among the trials that had not yet reached a boundary (Liu et al., 2026). For each evidence level, we multiplied its probability by the first-passage-time density of the second phase starting from that level, and integrated these products over all levels. The implementation and validation details are reported in Supplement S1.

The assumed ordering of the two signals is a modeling choice rather than an empirical conclusion. We fitted both the mean-first and the contrast-first version of the time-varying model.We reported the results from the mean-first model in the main analyses and compared the two orderings in the Results.

Model space

We compared three nested models, each adding one parameter to the previous model.

The baseline model used the mean reward-emotion signal as its only drift predictor (Fig. 1a). It estimated the mean-signal drift, the decision threshold, and the non-decision time. The contrast model additionally estimated a drift weight for the contrast signal (Fig. 1b). In this model, both signals drove the drift from the onset of evidence accumulation. The time-varying model additionally estimated the onset τ, so that the contrast signal entered evidence accumulation after an estimated delay (Fig. 1c). We compared the baseline and contrast models to test whether fit improved when the contrast signal was added. We compared the contrast and time-varying models to test whether fit improved further when the contrast signal entered after a delay.

For the primary analysis, we compared drift rate and decision threshold between groups in the baseline model. We repeated this comparison in the time-varying model to test whether the result depended on the model. We compared the onset τ between groups as an exploratory analysis.

Fig. 1 The three models in the model space. Schematic accumulation traces (grayscale) for each model, from the non-decision time to the Accept/Reject boundaries. a, The baseline model (time-stationary, three parameters), used for the primary analysis. The mean signal alone drives the drift. b, The contrast model (time-stationary, four parameters). A weight for the contrast signal is added, and both signals drive the drift from the onset of evidence accumulation. The dashed grey line shows the slope of the baseline model for comparison. c, The time-varying model (five parameters), used for the exploratory onset analysis. The mean signal alone drives the drift until the onset τ, when the contrast signal is added. Phase 1 and Phase 2 mark the intervals before and after τ. τ is expressed in seconds from the onset of evidence accumulation. The traces are illustrative.

Parameter estimation

We estimated each participant's parameters by maximum likelihood using differential evolution, as implemented in the R package DEoptim (Mullen et al., 2011). We used a population size of 80 and a maximum of 200 generations, with no early stopping before the generation limit. We fitted each participant independently and interpreted the estimates only at the group level, a two-stage approach in which participant-level estimates serve as the observations for the group comparison (Cohen et al., 2008; Estes & Maddox, 2005).

We fitted every participant ten times with different random seeds and kept the run that reached the highest likelihood (Supplement S2). Because the search is stochastic, different runs can converge to different parameter values. We computed quantities derived from the estimates, such as the proportion of estimates reaching a parameter bound, from the retained run for each participant.

We compared the groups on the participant-level estimates rather than fitting a hierarchical model, because contrast-weight estimates reached a parameter bound in 50.7% of the participants (Supplement S4). Hierarchical shrinkage would be difficult to interpret without stronger distributional assumptions (Katahira, 2016; Supplement S2). The predicted and the observed standard errors of the group difference can be found in Supplement S4.

Parameter bounds are listed in Supplement S1. We set the upper bound for non-decisiontime to 3.0 s after fitting the model at bounds from 1.5 to 3.5 s. We chose that range relative to the median choice response time of 3.2 s in this task. We chose 3.0 s because the median estimate no longer changed at bounds of 2.5 s and above (Supplement S3). We refitted the model at each of those bounds and checked the onset difference across them. The ceiling rate, the median non-decision time, and the group comparison at each bound can be found in Supplement S3. We estimated the non-decision time in every model without interpreting its group difference (Supplement S3). We allowed the onset τ to take negative values, which allows both signals to enter from the start of evidence accumulation. We counted an estimate as bounded when it fell within 0.05 of a box constraint, and we report the counts at a second tolerance of 0.001 to show how the classification depends on the criterion. We computed bound rates from the retained run for each participant.

Statistical analysis

We compared the groups on acceptance rate and median response time with Welch twosample t-tests. At the trial level, we fitted a logistic mixed model of acceptance (accept = 1) to the 6,739 retained trials. Its fixed effects were the mean signal, the contrast signal, group (high CES-D = 1, low CES-D = 0), and the two signal-by-group interactions. It included a random intercept and a random mean-signal slope for each participant. We fitted the model with lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) using the bobyqa optimizer.

We used nested model comparisons to evaluate the contribution of the contrast signal and its onset time. The contrast model was compared with the baseline model to test whether adding the contrast signal improved fit, and the time-varying model was compared with the contrast model to test whether freeing the contrast-signal onset improved fit beyond the contrast signal itself. We compared the models with the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), computed for each participant and averaged across participants.

We compared DDM parameters between the high and low depressive-symptom groups by Welch two-sample t-tests. All tests were two-tailed with alpha set at .05. Because several parameter distributions are bounded and right-skewed, we repeated the onset comparison with a rank-based Wilcoxon test. We report exact p-values, Cohen's d with 95% confidence interval, and, for the Wilcoxon test, the Hodges-Lehmann estimate of the shift.

We additionally tested whether any onset difference was separable from general slowing.

We regressed τ on the group while controlling for the threshold, the non-decision time, the common-signal drift, and the median response time, and repeated the model without the nondecision time. For the regression with all four covariates, we compared the models with and without the group term by a Bayes factor (BF01; Supplement S4) We also treated the CES-D total as a continuous measure, correlating each fitted parameter with it across all 351 participants, and repeated every group comparison with age and gender as covariates.

Identifiability and validation

We tested how well the parameters of the baseline and time-varying models could be recovered and how stable each group effect was across samples. We conducted six analyses, specified with their outcomes in Supplement S4 (Table S4).

First, we simulated data from both models at 20 and at 80 trials per participant and refitted each model with the same likelihood, to measure how well an individual parameter can be recovered at these trial counts. Second, we drew 30 random splits of participants into two halves, fitted each half independently, and took agreement in the sign of each group effect across the two halves as the index of stability. The other four analyses concern the onset in the time-varying model (Supplement S4). In three of them, we refitted simulated data in which we imposed a known onset difference, set that difference to zero, or replaced it with a starting-point difference. In the last analysis, we compared the response-time pattern simulated from the fitted model with the observed pattern.

Preregistration

This study reanalysed a publicly available dataset and was not preregistered. The drift and threshold comparisons test a pattern reported in prior work (Lawlor et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2024). We treat the onset analysis as exploratory.

Use of large language models

We used a large language model (Claude; Anthropic) as an editorial and coding assistant.

It was used to correct typographical and grammatical errors in the manuscript and to help optimize analysis scripts under the authors' direction. The authors developed the research idea and drafted the manuscript. All analyses were run and inspected by the authors, every reported statistic was regenerated from the archived fits, and every citation was verified against the source article by the authors. The authors take full responsibility for the content of the manuscript.

Results

Model-free comparison

Acceptance rates were comparable between the groups (0.719 in the low depressivesymptom group and 0.703 in the high depressive-symptom group; t(324) = -0.62, p = .53, d = -0.07). The high depressive-symptom group responded more slowly (median choice response time was 3.18 s and 3.67 s; t(278) = 4.21, p < .001, d = 0.46). In a trial-level logistic mixed model, acceptance in the high depressive-symptom group depended less on the mean signal (group × mean-signal interaction β = -0.54, SE = 0.23, p = .019). The contrast signal lowered acceptance in the low depressive-symptom group (β = -0.81, SE = 0.25) and had a slope near zero in the high depressive-symptom group (β = 0.26, SE = 0.19; difference 1.07, SE = 0.32, p < .001). With the CES-D total score treated as a continuous measure across all 351 participants, the pattern was the same. Higher CES-D total scores went with longer median response times (r(349) = 0.23, p < .001), but were uncorrelated with acceptance rates (r(349) = .00, p = .99).

Model Comparison

The time-stationary baseline model had a lower BIC than the time-varying model. The mean BIC difference was +1.95 per participant. The baseline model had the lowest BIC for 62.4% of the low depressive-symptom group and 68.5% of the high depressive-symptom group, whereas the time-varying model had the lowest BIC for 3.4% of the low depressive-symptom group and 7.5% of the high depressive-symptom group. These results suggest better fit for the baseline model among most participants On average, the likelihood gain from each added parameter fell short of its BIC penalty.

With both signals accumulating from the start of evidence accumulation, adding the contrast signal changed fit by a mean ΔBIC of +0.16 per participant, leaving the four-parameter contrast model marginally behind the three-parameter baseline. Freeing the onset then changed a mean ΔBIC by +1.79. This value was below zero for 10.0% of participants and below -2 for 2.8%, suggesting positive evidence favoring the time-varying model for only a small minority of participants (Kass & Raftery, 1995; Raftery, 1995; Fig. 3).

BIC favored the models without an onset. We therefore compare the drift rate and decision threshold between groups based on the baseline model. As an exploratory analysis, we also compare the onset between the two groups based on the time-varying model, although this result should be regarded as preliminary.

Depressive symptoms are associated with lower drift and greater caution

Depressive symptoms were associated with reduced sensitivity to the mean rewardemotion signal and with a wider decision threshold. In the time-stationary baseline model, the mean-signal drift was lower in the high depressive-symptom group (low CES-D = 0.677 vs high CES-D = 0.461, t(306) = 2.80, p = .005, d = 0.30, 95% CI [0.09, 0.52]; Fig. 3a). The high depressive-symptom group also had a wider decision threshold, so more evidence had to accumulate before a choice (low CES-D = 1.82 vs high CES-D = 2.00, t(303) = 3.63, p < .001, d = 0.40, 95% CI [0.18, 0.61]; Fig. 3b). The two differences held with the CES-D total treated as a continuous measure (drift r(349) = -0.18, threshold r(349) = 0.18, both p < .001; Supplement S5). They also held with age and gender as covariates (Supplement S6). The time-varying model gave the same result for the mean-signal drift (low CES-D = 0.737 vs high CES-D = 0.540, t(295) = 2.29, p = .023, d = 0.25, 95% CI [0.04, 0.47]). It also gave the same result for the threshold (low CES-D = 1.89 vs high CES-D = 2.06, t(315) = 3.39, p < .001, d = 0.37, 95% CI [0.15, 0.58]). The contrast weight differed little between the groups (low CES-D = 0.29 vs high CES-D = 0.24, t(332) = 0.17, p = .87, d = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.19, 0.23]). Choices simulated from the fitted parameters did not reproduce the group difference in the model-free contrast slope (Supplement S4). Onset estimates are those from the highest-likelihood run of ten optimizer runs per participant, with onsets at or below zero set to zero. Panel c has a dashed frame because the onset belongs to the exploratory analysis.

Drift and threshold were recoverable and stable across splits

The drift and threshold were recovered well in both models. At 20 trials per participant, generating and estimated values correlated in the baseline model at r = 0.90 for the drift and 0.87 for the threshold, and in the time-varying model at r = 0.88 and 0.85 (Supplement S4, Table S4).

At 80 trials, all four correlations were 0.96 or above. In the trials simulated with every onset set to the sample mean, the time-varying model estimated the group differences in drift and threshold within 0.03 of their generating sizes of 0.20 and 0.17 (Supplement S4, Table S6). In all 30 random splits of the sample, both independently fitted halves showed lower drift and a wider threshold in the high depressive-symptom group (baseline model; Fig. 4). The non-decision time was also recovered well (r = 0.97 at 20 trials in both models).

By contrast, at 20 trials, the contrast-weight and onset estimates correlated with their generating values at r = 0.39 and -0.02, respectively. At the group level, with four injected onset differences from 0 to 0.34 s at 20 trials per participant, the estimated onset difference rose with a slope of 0.38 (95% CI [0.22, 0.55]). When no difference was injected, the estimate was 0.16 s (Supplement S4, Table S7). When we inverted this relation at the observed 0.21 s, the 95% interval for the underlying onset difference included zero (-0.47 to 0.71 s; Supplement S4, Fig. S3c).

Discussion

This study used DDM to examine the decision processes underlying slower social decisions in people with elevated depressive symptoms. We found that although acceptance rates were comparable between the groups, the high depressive-symptom group responded more slowly. In the time-stationary DDM, the high depressive-symptom group showed reduced sensitivity to the mean reward-emotion signal and a wider decision threshold. The time-varying model yielded the same pattern for both parameters. In an exploratory analysis, depressive symptoms were associated with a later estimated onset of the reward-emotion contrast signal.

Together, these findings suggest that depression-related slowing during social decision-making reflects weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution.

These results are consistent with prior evidence of response slowing during social decision-making among individuals with elevated depressive symptoms (Fu et al., 2026). Using DDMs, previous studies have shown lower drift rates and wider thresholds among depressed participants in non-social reward tasks (Lawlor et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2024). The present study extends this decision-process profile to social decision-making, showing lower drift rates and wider decision thresholds in an ultimatum game. Previous work interpreted slower responding during the ultimatum game as psychomotor slowing (Fu et al., 2026). In the present data, the slower responses went together with weaker evidence accumulation and a wider threshold. The decision-process differences reported in non-social tasks may therefore also account for the slower responses of people with depression in social decisions.

Some recent evidence suggests that different attributes may enter decision processes at different time points (Maier et al., 2020; Sullivan & Huettel, 2021), and such onset differences may be altered in clinical populations (Shevlin et al., 2025). We therefore conducted an exploratory time-varying DDM analysis in the current study. In this model, the mean signal drives evidence accumulation from the beginning of the decision process, whereas the contrast signal enters after an onset time. We found that the estimated onset of the contrast signal was later in the high depressive-symptom group than in the low depressive-symptom group.

However, this result should be treated as preliminary, since the time-varying DDM had a higher BIC than the standard DDM. One potential issue limiting the advantage and interpretability of the time-varying model is that the reward and emotion prediction errors were highly correlated, so they could not be treated as fully independent attributes. The mean-contrast decomposition therefore captures the shared and differentiating components of the two prediction errors, but the contrast signal varies over a narrow range, which leaves its weight and onset weakly determined in some participants (Supplement S1). Future studies should confirm this finding in designs with more independent reward and emotion prediction-error signals, or with additional process measures that can independently validate attribute-onset timing.

These findings have several theoretical and clinical implications. First, these results suggest that comparable choices in high and low depressive-symptom groups can arise from different latent decision processes. In the ultimatum game, acceptance rates did not differ between groups, but DDMs indicated weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution in participants with elevated depressive symptoms. Therefore, social decision-making in depression may be altered even when overt choices appear intact. Second, the results refine the interpretation of depression-related response slowing. Slower social decisions may reflect reduced efficiency in accumulating evidence and greater decision caution, rather than global psychomotor slowing alone (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008; Weigard et al., 2026). Third, these process-level measures may serve as candidate markers for future intervention studies. For example, interventions aimed at improving social functioning in individuals elevated depressive symptoms could examine whether these individuals show increased evidence-accumulation efficiency, reduced excessive caution, or both. Although these applications remain preliminary, DDM parameters may help link depressive symptoms to specific cognitive processes that contribute to social impairment and may provide measurable targets for future mechanistic treatment research.

This study also has some limitations. First, because the groups were defined by a selfreport symptom scale, the results apply to elevated depressive symptoms rather than to clinically diagnosed depression. Second, the monetary and emotional information were available at the same time in the current task. Mouse tracking (Maier et al., 2020) or a task that presents the two kinds of information at different times would provide an independent check of the estimated onset. Third, the onset difference should be interpreted with caution. The time-varying DDM did not provide a clear improvement in fit after accounting for model complexity, and individual onset estimates were not reliably recovered at the current trial count. Thus, the onset parameter should be interpreted at the group level rather than as a stable individual-difference measure.

Finally, the neural mechanisms underlying these process-level alterations remain unclear. Future studies could use event-related potentials or functional neuroimaging techniques to examine the neural correlates of weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution during social decision-making in individuals with elevated depressive symptoms.

In summary, this study used DDMs to examine cognitive mechanisms underlying social decision-making and their associations with depressive symptoms. In the ultimatum game, the high depressive-symptom group responded more slowly than the low depressive-symptom group and accepted offers at a comparable rate. Their slower responses were accompanied by a lower drift rate and a wider decision threshold, suggesting weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution, respectively. An exploratory time-varying model estimated a later onset of the reward-emotion contrast signal in the high depressive-symptom group. We read this delay as part of a broader slowing of the decision. Together, these results suggest that DDMs of social decision-making can elucidate the computational components underlying depression-related slowing. Drift rate and decision threshold may provide candidate process-level mechanisms for future intervention studies aimed at improving social decision-making difficulties associated with depressive symptoms.

Author contributions

Jinil Kim curated the data, developed the methodology and software, performed the formal analysis, validation, and visualization, and wrote the original draft. Yuan-Wei Yao conceived the

Exploratory analysis: a later estimated onset of the contrast signal

The estimated onset of the contrast signal was later in the high depressive-symptom group (τ: low CES-D = 0.80 s vs high CES-D = 1.01 s, t(299) = 2.02, p = .044, d = 0.22, 95% CI [0.01, 0.43]), a fitted delay of 0.21 s (Fig. 3c). In all 30 random splits of the sample, both independently fitted halves showed a later onset in the high depressive-symptom group (Fig. 4).

Higher CES-D totals were associated with later estimated onsets (r(349) = 0.13, p = .014; Supplement S5). With age and gender as covariates, the delay was 0.24 s (p = .024; Supplement S6). In five further analyses with other model settings, a rank-based test, or participant subsets, the high depressive-symptom group again showed a later estimated onset (Supplement S3 and S4).

However, group differences in the other parameters and in response time could account for most of the delay. When we simulated all participants' trials with each onset set to the sample mean of 0.89 s and the other parameters at their fitted values, the delay estimated from these trials was 0.13 s, 63% of the observed 0.21 s (Supplement S4, Fig. S2b). With the threshold, nondecision time, mean-signal drift, and median response time as covariates, the adjusted delay was 0.08 s (95% CI [-0.12, 0.28], p = .442, BF01 = 3.38; Supplement S4, Fig. S2a). We therefore read the delay as a temporal component of general slowing rather than as a separate dimension.
